abstract: Upgrades an existing Gradle wrapper to a target version on Gradle 7.0 through 9.x. Orients first — confirms the wrapper is present and reads both the declared version and the distribution type from gradle-wrapper.properties — then resolves the target version (defaulting to the latest release when the user names none), sources that distribution's SHA-256, records a baseline by running the tasks task on the current version, secures the four wrapper files — relying on a clean git worktree where there is one and falling back to a copy outside the project tree otherwise — and runs the built-in wrapper task twice with the version and checksum pinned, so that gradlew, gradlew.bat, and gradle-wrapper.jar are regenerated from the new version's templates rather than the old ones. Verification is by diff rather than by version string, because a half-done upgrade still reports the new version, and is then followed by re-running the tasks canary on the new version. A file-level upgrade that lands correctly and leaves a build that no longer configures is treated as a failed job rather than a successful one, which is the case the canary exists to catch. Two reference files carry the branches most upgrades never reach — references/snapshot.md for securing and restoring the wrapper where git cannot, and references/rollback.md for the rollback procedure itself — each opened only when its case arises, so the cost of carrying them falls on the runs that need them: all four files are restored — by git checkout, or from the copy in a single tree-preserving cp, never as a list of four paths, which silently flattens the properties and jar into the project root — and the restore is verified by re-running the canary, with a failing canary at that point treated as a bad restore to be fixed rather than a second finding. A restore means the upgrade did not happen, so no wording of the report may describe it as completed, and every fact in the report is re-read from the project after the last restore rather than quoted from an earlier reading that a failed run or a bad restore has since invalidated. The closing message must carry four things: the verdict that the build does not appear to be upgradeable to the version named, the failure text quoted, the next minor release offered as a smaller step — or an explicit statement that no smaller step exists, so that the item is never satisfied by silence — and links to that version's release notes at docs.gradle.org plus, for a major, its upgrade guide. The smaller hop is recommended, never performed. Explains the run-it-twice gotcha and the symptoms of a half-done upgrade, why a snapshot must cover the scripts and jar rather than the properties alone and must live outside the project, why the canary is tasks rather than build and what configuration-on-demand does to it, the rule that an upgrade must preserve the existing bin or all distribution type, how to pick the right checksum among the ones published per release, the checksum rules that apply once distributionSha256Sum is set, the version labels accepted by --gradle-version, and the Gradle 9 requirement that gradle-wrapper.properties declare a full X.Y.Z version. Distinguishes 'upgrade it' (execute) from 'how do I upgrade' (hand over the commands), and draws its rollback line at the build phase rather than the command: a build that no longer configures is rolled back, while an execution-phase failure such as a compile error or a failing test is left in place and reported. Deliberately narrow: it does not add a wrapper to a project that has none, configure authenticated distributions, customize the Wrapper task, or repair a build in either direction — neither to force a blocked upgrade through nor to fix what the new version broke.
